explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Paul opens by calling himself "an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God" (Colossians 1:1). He doesn't say he picked the job or applied for it. He says it came by God's will, and I'm just a stamper who got called out of a drawer, so I get that.

Paul says it plainly: he is "an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God" (Colossians 1:1). So the letter's own first line says yes to this one. He doesn't claim he got there on his own. Right out of the gate, he points to God's will.

Thank is it. Paul writes, "We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you" (Colossians 1:3). Notice the word always. Nobody's tapping a watch here, because thanks is where the prayer starts.

Paul doesn't say they question God. He says, "We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you" (Colossians 1:3). I'd say that's a much better way to open a prayer than a list of complaints. Thanks is the word.

Remind is a fair guess, since a lot of us treat prayer like a to-do list. But Paul says, "We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you" (Colossians 1:3). The word is thank. No reminders needed.

Faith is right, baker. Paul says they've heard about "your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints" (Colossians 1:4). Two things in one sentence: trusting Christ and loving His people. Word travels about that kind of thing.

Wisdom sounds nice, but it's not the word here. Paul says, "your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints" (Colossians 1:4). Wisdom does show up later, when he prays for them in verse 9. For this blank, it's faith.

Boldness is a good trait, but Paul doesn't name it here. He says what he heard was "your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints" (Colossians 1:4). So the word is faith. It's the trust in Christ that got talked about.
In heaven, baker. Paul calls it "the hope stored up for you in heaven" (Colossians 1:5). It's kept safe up there, and nobody down here can lose it for them. That's a storage unit I'd trust.

Jerusalem is a real city, but it's not where Paul puts this hope. He says it's "stored up for you in heaven" (Colossians 1:5). The Colossians were at Colossae, and their hope wasn't tied to a map location. It's kept in heaven.

The temple was a big deal in the Bible, but Paul doesn't say it holds this hope. He says it's "stored up for you in heaven" (Colossians 1:5). Heaven is the answer. That's a whole different level of safekeeping.
That's the one. Paul says, "All over the world this gospel is bearing fruit and growing" (Colossians 1:6). Bearing fruit and growing, both at once. That's a gospel with no brakes.
Nope, Paul says the opposite. "All over the world this gospel is bearing fruit and growing" (Colossians 1:6). Nothing about slowing or fading anywhere in that line. The gospel is on the move.

Paul doesn't describe the gospel as waiting around. He says, "All over the world this gospel is bearing fruit and growing" (Colossians 1:6). It's already out there, already doing its work. Bearing fruit and growing is the answer.

Not quite, baker. Paul says the gospel has been bearing fruit and growing among them "since the day you heard it and truly understood the grace of God" (Colossians 1:6). That's since the day, not years later. So the statement is false.

False is right. Paul says the gospel has been bearing fruit and growing among the Colossians "since the day you heard it and truly understood the grace of God" (Colossians 1:6). No years of waiting are mentioned. It started the day they heard and understood.

Epaphras it is. Paul says, "You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant" (Colossians 1:7). He's also called a faithful minister of Christ on Paul's behalf. Paul gives him a good name, and I'd take that over a price sticker any day.

Barnabas was a real companion of Paul's, but he isn't the name in this verse. Paul says, "You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant" (Colossians 1:7). So the Colossians heard the gospel from Epaphras. Good guess on a familiar name, though.

Silas was another friend of Paul's, but he isn't named here. Paul says, "You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant" (Colossians 1:7). Epaphras is the one who taught them. Silas will have to wait for another letter.
Spirit, yes. Paul says Epaphras "also informed us of your love in the Spirit" (Colossians 1:8). Epaphras brought good news back, and that was part of it. A good report is a gift.

Law is a word you'll see a lot in the Bible, but it's not in this verse. Paul says Epaphras "informed us of your love in the Spirit" (Colossians 1:8). The blank is Spirit. Their love was in the Spirit.
Church seems like a safe guess, but Paul words it differently. He says Epaphras "informed us of your love in the Spirit" (Colossians 1:8). The missing word is Spirit. That's the word Paul picked.

Yes. Paul says he's been "asking God to fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding" (Colossians 1:9). He's not asking for a little. He's asking for FILLED. I'd say that's the kind of prayer that sticks.

That's not what Paul asks for. He prays that God would "fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding" (Colossians 1:9). The request is knowing God's will, not dreading judgment. Spiritual wisdom and understanding come with it.

Prophecy is a real gift in the Bible, but it isn't what Paul asks for here. He prays that God would "fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding" (Colossians 1:9). So the answer is the knowledge of His will.

explanations.answer: So they may walk worthy of the Lord
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul prays "so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way" (Colossians 1:10). Knowing God's will is meant to show up in how they live. Knowing and walking go together.

explanations.answer: So they may win every argument
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. The knowledge is "so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way" (Colossians 1:10). It's about how they live, not winning debates. I've lost plenty of arguments with my own mustache and I'm doing fine.

explanations.answer: So they may earn God's love
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't put it that way. He says the knowledge is "so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way" (Colossians 1:10). Nothing there says they're earning anything. The goal is walking worthy of the Lord.
Close, but not what the text says. Paul prays they "may please Him in every way" (Colossians 1:10). Every way, not a few important ones. So this one is false.
False is right. Paul prays they "may please Him in every way" (Colossians 1:10). Not a few ways, every way. He keeps the prayer wide open.

Right. Paul prays they'll be "strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience" (Colossians 1:11). The power is for lasting and waiting well. That's the kind of strength I could use during a long bake.

Paul doesn't mention enemies here. He prays they'll be "strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience" (Colossians 1:11). The strength is for endurance and patience.

Signs and wonders appear elsewhere in the Bible, but Paul doesn't ask for them here. He prays they'll be "strengthened with all power according to His glorious might so that you may have full endurance and patience" (Colossians 1:11). So the answer is endurance and patience.

True. Paul says the Father "has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light" (Colossians 1:12). Notice who does the qualifying: the Father. The Colossians didn't have to qualify themselves.

This one is actually true. Paul says the Father "has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light" (Colossians 1:12). The Father did the qualifying. That's good news for anybody worried about their own résumé.

Darkness, baker. Paul says, "He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son" (Colossians 1:13). Rescued out and brought in. I know a little about being pulled out of the dark, and it never gets old.

Egypt is a real rescue story in the Bible, but it isn't the word here. Paul says, "He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son" (Colossians 1:13). The blank is darkness.

Sickness is a real struggle, but that's not what Paul names. He says, "He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son" (Colossians 1:13). The word is darkness. And He brings us into the Son's kingdom.

Forgiveness, yes. Paul says, "in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" (Colossians 1:14). We have it in the Son. That's the best thing I've ever heard, and I've heard the oven timer go off.
Memory is a nice-sounding word, but it's not the one Paul uses. He says, "in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" (Colossians 1:14). The blank is forgiveness. That's what redemption is.
Record is a tricky one, but Paul doesn't say it. He writes, "in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" (Colossians 1:14). So the word is forgiveness. That's what we have in the Son.
